section_summary: Pages 1–38 are a State Department “List of Papers” indexing records on Japanese budgets, public finance, foreign borrowing, exchange controls, gold movements, and war-related expenditures from 1931 through 1938. The remaining pages contain January–February 1932 records describing Japan’s deteriorating external position after abandonment of the gold standard, including a Kobe consular report, an Embassy discussion of the gold embargo and alleged Mitsui speculation, and Thomas W. Lamont’s refusal to contemplate a Japanese loan. Cross-reference sheets also connect the file to reports on South Manchurian Railway financing and other Japanese financial records.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Financial Affairs—Japan
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Indexes State Department records concerning Japanese finance, budgets, loans, exchange controls, gold movements, and war expenditures from 1931 through 1938.
subfiles.summary: This continuation of the file’s list of papers supplies numbered entries, dates, senders, and abstracts for diplomatic telegrams, despatches, memoranda, correspondence, reports, and cross-references. The entries trace Japan’s abandonment of the gold standard, budget deficits, bond issues, foreign-loan rumors, military spending in Manchuria and China, and increasingly stringent exchange and capital controls. Later entries document American and European debate over denying Japan credit during the Sino-Japanese conflict.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Note on Japan’s Foreign Balances and Obligations
subfiles.about: Requests a clearer special report connecting Japan’s accumulated dollar and sterling holdings with its foreign-currency obligations.
subfiles.summary: The writer finds the underlying despatch unclear because it separately discusses Japanese accumulations of dollars and pounds and the obligations payable in those currencies without connecting the two. The note asks to whom the Yokohama Specie Bank is indebted and suggests requesting a special report. It adds that Castle is writing Lamont of Morgan’s about any possible Japanese approach and might be interested in the despatch.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Financial Position in 1932, as Seen by Kobe and Osaka Bankers
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, U.S. Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s external-payment position, specie reserve, maturing foreign debts, export prospects, and likely borrowing needs after abandonment of the gold standard.
subfiles.summary: Dickover reports heavy Japanese purchases of dollars and sterling during late 1931, driven by import requirements, capital flight, and expectations of yen depreciation. Gold exports covered much of the movement, but Japan retained large uncovered commitments while its specie reserve fell sharply; the Yokohama Specie Bank alone had substantial New York borrowings, and South Manchurian Railway and Toho Electric bonds were soon to mature. Shipping receipts, exports, and China trade were weakened by sterling depreciation and the Chinese boycott, making export bills inadequate to cover foreign payments. Kobe and Osaka bankers expected attempts to borrow in New York, London, or Paris, but believed poor public finances, inflationary policies, and the Manchurian affair would make credit scarce or expensive.

subfiles.title: Document File Note for Despatch No. 458
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy in Japan (W. Cameron Forbes)
subfiles.about: Cross-references Forbes’s discussion of the gold-conversion prohibition, declining exchange rate, and alleged Mitsui dollar intrigue.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs users from file 894.51/324 to despatch no. 458 in 894.00 P.R./49. It identifies the subjects as Japan’s prohibition of note conversion into gold, depreciation of exchange, and allegations that Mitsui interests profited from dollar speculation.

subfiles.title: Fragment of Despatch No. 458 on the Gold Embargo and Mitsui Dollar Intrigue
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains Japan’s return to a gold embargo and reports rumors that Mitsui interests profited from the associated depreciation of the yen.
subfiles.summary: The fragment attributes the embargo to Seiyūkai policy, depletion of Japan’s gold reserve, Britain’s suspension of gold conversion, budgetary imbalance, depressed trade, and economic advocacy. An imperial ordinance prohibited the Banks of Japan, Chosen, and Taiwan from converting notes into gold without Finance Ministry permission, after which the yen fell sharply. It also records widely believed but unverified allegations that Mitsui interests bought dollars in anticipation of the embargo and earned about ¥60 million, provoking limited proletarian demonstrations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Thomas W. Lamont
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Records Lamont’s categorical statement that New York financial interests would not lend money to Japan under prevailing conditions.
subfiles.summary: Castle asked whether Japan’s financial difficulties might lead it to seek further American advances. Lamont replied that no request had yet been made and that any such request would have no prospect of success. He described Japan as poor security because of collapsing trade and departure from the gold standard and stated firmly that New York would lend Japan nothing at that time.

subfiles.title: Strictly Confidential Letter Enclosing the Lamont Memorandum for Ambassador Forbes
subfiles.from: Secretary of State, signed for by William R. Castle Jr.
subfiles.to: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards confidentially a copy of the memorandum of Castle’s January 28 conversation with Thomas W. Lamont.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends Ambassador Forbes a copy of the memorandum recording the Under Secretary’s conversation with Lamont. The letter marks the enclosure and its contents as strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Strictly Confidential Letter Enclosing the Lamont Memorandum for Minister Johnson
subfiles.from: Secretary of State, signed for by William R. Castle Jr.
subfiles.to: Nelson T. Johnson, U.S. Minister, Peiping
subfiles.about: Forwards confidentially a copy of the memorandum of Castle’s January 28 conversation with Thomas W. Lamont.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends Minister Johnson a copy of the Lamont memorandum for his strictly confidential information. The enclosure conveyed New York financial opposition to extending a loan to Japan.

subfiles.title: Document File Note on South Manchurian Railway Construction and Prospective American Loans
subfiles.about: Cross-references a memorandum suggesting that new South Manchurian Railway construction orders might be offered in exchange for American financing.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points from file 894.51/326 to memorandum 893.77/2832. Its abstract states that extensive South Manchurian Railway construction would require railway-material orders that might be used as inducements for loans in the American market.
